$$ \text{molecular mass of solute} = M $$ 

Then $w = \frac{SVM}{1000}$ 

To solve the molarity related problem, we can use the above equation

**Problem:** How will you prepare $0.2 \text{ molar } \text{NaCl}$ solution in a volumetric flask of $250 \text{ mL}$?

**Solution:** Given, a volume of solution $V = 250 \text{ mL}$, molarity of solution $S = 0.2 \text{ molar}$, molecular mass of $\text{NaCl} = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5$

Therefore, $1 \text{ mole } \text{NaCl} = 58.5 \text{ g}$

$0.2 \text{ molar } \text{NaCl}$ solution in $1 \text{ liter}$ or $1000 \text{ mL}$ requires $58.5 \times 0.2 = 11.7 \text{ g}$

$250 \text{ mL}$ solution requires $= \frac{11.7 \times 250}{1000} = 2.925 \text{ g}$

Add $2.925 \text{ gram } \text{NaCl}$ in a $250 \text{ mL}$ volumetric flask. Pour $250 \text{ mL}$ water inside the flask. That will complete the preparation of $0.2 \text{ molar}$ solution.

**Alternative Solution**

We know, $w = \frac{SVM}{1000}$

Therefore, $w = \frac{0.2 \times 250 \times 58.5}{1000} = 2.925 \text{ g}$

Now, follow the procedure of adding the solute and solvent to complete the preparation.

**Problem:** How much $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ is there in a $2 \text{ liter } 0.1 \text{ molar } \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ solution?

**Solution:** Molecular mass of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = 23 \times 2 + 12 + 16 \times 3 = 106$

Therefore, the amount of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ necessary in a $1 \text{ liter } 1 \text{ molar}$ solution $= 106 \text{ g}$

the amount of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ necessary in a $1 \text{ liter } 0.1 \text{ molar}$ solution $= 10.6 \text{ g}$

the amount of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ necessary in a $2 \text{ liter } 0.1 \text{ molar}$ solution $= 10.6 \times 2 \text{ g} = 21.2 \text{ g}$
